pois.name: Al-Ma'mun's Tunnel
pois.blurb: The Robbers' Tunnel — forced through the core masonry, by tradition for Caliph al-Ma'mun around AD 820. It is how every visitor enters today.

pois.name: The granite plugs
pois.blurb: Three granite blocks slid down to seal the Ascending Passage. The tunnellers cut round them through the softer limestone — and so found the upper chambers.

pois.name: Descending Passage
pois.blurb: Descending Passage — 105 m at 26.5°, only 1.05 m wide and 1.2 m high, so straight that its sides stray barely 6 mm over its masonry-built part. Crouch (C).

pois.name: Ascending Passage
pois.blurb: Ascending Passage — 39 m at 26°, the same cramped 1.05 × 1.2 m section; visitors climb it bent double on a cleated wooden ramp.

pois.name: Queen's Chamber passage
pois.blurb: A level passage 38.7 m long and 1.17 m high; the floor drops half a metre for the last 5.5 m before the chamber.

pois.name: Queen's Chamber
pois.blurb: Queen's Chamber — fine limestone under a gabled roof, 5.76 × 5.23 m and 6.23 m to the ridge, exactly on the pyramid's east–west axis. No queen was buried here; the name is a later guess.

pois.name: The corbelled niche
pois.blurb: A niche 4.67 m high in the east wall, stepping inward in five corbels — perhaps for a statue of the king. Treasure hunters hacked the rough tunnel in its back.

pois.name: Subterranean Chamber
pois.blurb: Subterranean Chamber — cut in the bedrock 30 m below the pyramid and abandoned unfinished: the western half is still a mass of rock fins and quarrymen's trenches.

pois.name: The pit
pois.blurb: A square pit in the chamber floor, deepened to some 11 m in 1837 by Howard Vyse, who hoped to find a hidden room below.

pois.name: Well shaft (lower mouth)
pois.blurb: The lower end of the "well": a rough shaft that climbs through the bedrock, past a natural grotto, to the foot of the Grand Gallery.

models.title: Great Pyramid — Grand Gallery and King's Chamber

pois.name: Grand Gallery
pois.blurb: Grand Gallery — 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high, its walls stepping inward in seven corbels to a roof only ~1 m wide. A 1 m channel runs between two ramps cut with 27 pairs of slots, whose purpose is still argued over.

pois.name: Antechamber
pois.blurb: Antechamber — granite, with the "granite leaf" hanging across it and three slots that held portcullis slabs, lowered to seal the King's Chamber. The passages either side are true size, 1.05 × 1.11 m — crouch (C) to get through.

pois.name: King's Chamber
pois.blurb: King's Chamber — 10.47 × 5.23 m and 5.85 m high, walled in 100 blocks of red Aswan granite, roofed by nine granite beams of up to ~80 tonnes. Two narrow shafts rise from the north and south walls.

pois.name: Khufu's sarcophagus
pois.blurb: A lidless granite coffer, 2.28 × 0.98 × 1.05 m — slightly wider than the passage, so it was set in place as the chamber was built. One corner was broken away by early visitors.

pois.name: Campbell's Chamber
pois.blurb: The topmost of five relieving chambers stacked above the King's Chamber, forced open with gunpowder by Howard Vyse in 1837. Its gabled blocks carry builders' red-ochre graffiti — including the cartouche of Khufu.

pois.name: Khafre — upper passage
pois.blurb: The upper entrance passage: rough-dressed red granite, 1.05 m wide and 1.2 m high, descending at 25°55′. Its flaws were made good with plaster and painted red.

pois.name: Khafre — granite portcullis
pois.blurb: A granite slab sliding in grooves cut in the passage walls. Perring attacked it in 1837, hoping for a passage above it; it now rests on rough limestone props.

pois.name: Khafre — horizontal passage
pois.blurb: From the portcullis the passage runs level to the chamber, half as high again (1.8 m): fine picked limestone at first, then rock, plastered over.

pois.name: Khafre — where the passages meet
pois.blurb: The lower passage rises through the floor here. When Belzoni reached this spot in 1818 he found a drop, and a second passage running away north and down.

pois.name: Khafre's burial chamber
pois.blurb: The great chamber — 14.17 × 4.97 m, cut in the rock and stuccoed, under a gable of limestone beams. The paving was torn up by Perring in 1837, looking for other rooms; the blocks still lie against the east wall.

pois.name: Khafre's sarcophagus
pois.blurb: A polished granite coffer, 2.63 × 1.07 m, sunk into the floor up to its sliding lid, which was pinned and cemented shut — and wrenched off all the same. The lid lies beside it.

pois.name: Belzoni's inscription
pois.blurb: "Scoperta da G. Belzoni. 2. mar. 1818" — painted across the south wall by Giovanni Belzoni the day he found the way in. Arabic graffiti showed him he was not the first.

pois.name: Khafre — lower chamber
pois.blurb: A second, rock-cut chamber, 10.46 × 3.13 m under a pent roof, reached by a short slope from the lower passage — perhaps a first burial chamber, perhaps a store.

pois.name: Khafre — turning recess
pois.blurb: A recess opposite the way into the lower chamber: room to swing a coffin round the right-angled turn.

pois.name: Khafre — lower passage
pois.blurb: The lower entrance, cut in the pavement north of the pyramid and running wholly through the rock. It is the way visitors go in today.

pois.name: Menkaure — Panelled Chamber
pois.blurb: Panelled Chamber — its rock walls, sides and ends, are carved as a palace façade: the first decoration inside any pyramid since Djoser. The passages are true size (about 1.05 × 1.2 m): crouch (C) to move on.

pois.name: Menkaure — Large Chamber
pois.blurb: The second chamber, 14.23 × 3.86 m and 4.87 m high — the burial room of the first design; two rock pilasters mark off its west end. High in the north wall opens the abandoned passage of that design; in the floor, a ramp leads down west to the final burial chamber.

pois.name: Menkaure — Burial Chamber
pois.blurb: Burial Chamber — lined with red granite under granite beams recut into a vault. The basalt sarcophagus Vyse found here in 1837, carved as a palace façade, was lost at sea in 1838 when the Beatrice sank off Spain.

pois.name: Menkaure — Room of the six niches
pois.blurb: Down six steps — the oldest known flight of steps in any building, Petrie thought: a rock-cut room with six deep loculi, four in the east wall and two in the north, each over 2.5 m deep.

pois.name: Tomb of Meresankh III
pois.blurb: The rock-cut chapel of Queen Meresankh III, granddaughter of Khufu and wife of Khafre, found by Reisner in 1927 with its paint still bright. Her mother Hetepheres II gave her this tomb.

pois.name: The ten women
pois.blurb: Ten women carved from the living rock along the north wall — Meresankh, her mother Hetepheres II and her daughters — under an architrave naming the queen. Nothing quite like it survives in any other tomb.

pois.name: Offering room
pois.blurb: The west room: statue niches, a false door, and the shaft down to the burial chamber where her black granite sarcophagus (now in Cairo) was found.

pois.name: The scribes in the wall
pois.blurb: Three small niches low in the south wall hold rock-cut figures of scribes — thought to be the steward Khemetnu, who oversaw the making of the tomb, his son, and four grandsons.

pois.name: Burial chamber of Meresankh III
pois.blurb: Down a 5.1 m pit: the burial chamber, 5.7 m long and under 2 m high. Her black granite sarcophagus — a gift from her mother Hetepheres II, re-inscribed for her — stood by the west wall with its lid propped up, as here.

pois.name: Serapeum of Saqqara — Greater Vaults
pois.blurb: The catacombs of the sacred Apis bulls, begun under Psamtik I (664–610 BC) and extended by the Ptolemies to ~350 m. Twenty-four colossal stone sarcophagi stand in vaulted side chambers. Rediscovered by Auguste Mariette in 1850.

pois.name: Lid of Amasis II's sarcophagus
pois.blurb: The lid of the oldest hard-stone sarcophagus (c. 550 BC), moved to the entrance. Its inscription: "…he dedicated his monument to the Living Apis, a great sarcophagus of granite."

pois.name: Sarcophagus of Amasis II
pois.blurb: Red granite, finely worked with palace-facade panelling and a band of Pyramid Texts round the top; the signs were painted green. For the Apis that died in year 23 of Amasis II.

pois.name: Sarcophagus of Cambyses II
pois.blurb: Grey granite, dedicated c. 524 BC by the first Persian ruler of Egypt — "to his father Apis-Osiris". Only the lid is inscribed. It stands where it blocks the original entrance.

pois.name: Sarcophagus of Khabash
pois.blurb: A smaller box in an unused tunnel, dated to year 2 of the rebel king Khabash (c. 336 BC). Its lid was found on the floor nearby — the two may never have closed over a bull.

pois.name: The inscribed Ptolemaic sarcophagus
pois.blurb: Polished black stone with decoration merely scratched on: panelling, Pyramid Text spells — and royal cartouches left EMPTY, as nobody knew under which ruler this Apis would die.

pois.name: An Apis sarcophagus
pois.blurb: A typical box: 3.85 × 2.32 × 2.32 m with a 0.98 m lid — about 62 tonnes with its lid — let into a pit in a chamber whose floor is 2–3 m below the gallery. It took 28 working days to move one in (stela of year 37 of Ptolemy II).

pois.name: Luxor Corniche
pois.blurb: The East Bank river front: a stone embankment with the promenade above and the lower quay, where the boats lie, below.

pois.name: The Nile at Luxor
pois.blurb: The river here is about half a kilometre wide and flows north. Since the High Dam (1970) it no longer floods; its level changes by only a metre or two through the year.

pois.name: Nile cruise ships
pois.blurb: The Luxor–Aswan "floating hotels": about 72 m long and 14 m in beam, three cabin decks under a sun deck. There are so many that they moor two and three abreast, and passengers walk through one ship to reach the next.

pois.name: Feluccas
pois.blurb: Open wooden passenger sailboats with a single lateen sail on a very long yard — the traditional way to drift on the river at sunset. Press E beside the one at the steps to go out.

pois.name: Dahabiya
pois.blurb: A two-masted lateen houseboat: the way nineteenth-century travellers went up the Nile, revived today as small, quiet cruise boats, usually towed by a tug when the wind fails.

pois.name: National ferry
pois.blurb: The public ferry to the West Bank, used by townspeople and by visitors bound for the Valley of the Kings. Small covered motor launches make the same crossing for hire.

pois.name: Luxor Temple
pois.blurb: The pylon of Ramesses II, 65 m wide and 24 m high, with two seated colossi of the king and one obelisk of red granite — its twin has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since 1836. The massing here is schematic.

pois.name: Colonnade of Amenhotep III
pois.blurb: Fourteen papyrus columns nearly 16 m high in two rows: the processional way along which the barques of Amun, Mut and Khonsu were carried at the Opet festival.

pois.name: Mosque of Abu al-Haggag
pois.blurb: A mosque built in the thirteenth century on top of the then-buried court of Ramesses II, and still in use: when the temple was dug out, it was left standing high on the old ground level.

pois.name: Avenue of Sphinxes
pois.blurb: The sphinx-lined processional road that runs 2.7 km north from here to the temples of Karnak, reopened along its whole length in 2021.

pois.name: Winter Palace
pois.blurb: The Winter Palace hotel of 1907, ochre-fronted, on the corniche south of the temple. Lord Carnarvon stayed here, and it was on its noticeboard that news of Tutankhamun's tomb was posted in 1922.

pois.name: West Bank landing
pois.blurb: The landing at al-Gezira: beyond the fields the road runs to the Colossi of Memnon and the Theban necropolis.

pois.name: KV62 — Tomb of Tutankhamun
pois.blurb: The entrance Howard Carter's workmen uncovered on 4 November 1922, under the debris of huts built for the cutting of KV9 just above. The whitewashed walls, the roof over the stair and the gate are modern.

pois.name: Visitor centre
pois.blurb: The visitor centre at the mouth of the wadi: tickets, a large model of the valley and its tombs, and the booth for the "taf-taf", the little road train that carries visitors the last half-kilometre.

pois.name: al-Qurn
pois.blurb: Al-Qurn, "the Horn": the pyramid-shaped peak, about 450 m above sea level, that stands over the valley — perhaps the reason the kings chose this wadi for their tombs.

pois.name: Valley of the Kings
pois.blurb: The wadi where the pharaohs of the New Kingdom (c. 1539–1075 BC) were buried in rock-cut tombs — sixty-five are numbered. The pyramid-shaped peak above is al-Qurn.

pois.name: KV9 — Ramesses V and VI
pois.blurb: Entrance of KV9, the tomb of Ramesses V and VI, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.name: KV17 — Seti I
pois.blurb: Entrance of KV17, the tomb of Seti I, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV11, the tomb of Ramesses III, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV2, the tomb of Ramesses IV, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV6, the tomb of Ramesses IX, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV8, the tomb of Merenptah, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV14, the tomb of Tausret and Setnakht, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV35, the tomb of Amenhotep II, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV16, the tomb of Ramesses I, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV57, the tomb of Horemheb, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV5, the tomb of the sons of Ramesses II, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.blurb: Entrance of KV1, the tomb of Ramesses VII, placed from the Theban Mapping Project survey. Its interior is not built yet.

pois.name: Entrance stair
pois.blurb: Sixteen steps cut down into the valley floor. The lowest six were hacked away in antiquity to bring in the sarcophagus and shrines, and again by Carter to bring them out.

pois.name: Corridor
pois.blurb: A plain descending corridor, 8 m long. It was filled with limestone chips after the tomb was first robbed, and the robbers who came back tunnelled through the fill.

pois.name: Antechamber
pois.blurb: Antechamber — 7.85 × 3.55 m. Here Carter saw "wonderful things": dismantled chariots, three gilded couches, chests and the two guardian statues that flanked the sealed door to the burial chamber.

pois.name: Tutankhamun
pois.blurb: The king himself. Since 2007 his mummy has lain here in a climate-controlled case, rather than in the sarcophagus.

pois.name: Annexe
pois.blurb: A low doorway leads to the annexe, its floor nearly a metre lower — a store room found heaped with furniture, jars of wine and oils, and baskets of food.

pois.name: Burial chamber
pois.blurb: Burial chamber — 6.37 × 4.02 m, the only decorated room. Four gilded shrines, one inside another, almost filled it. The floor is nearly a metre below the antechamber; visitors look down from the platform.

pois.name: Sarcophagus
pois.blurb: Carved from a single block of quartzite, with a goddess at each corner spreading her wings. The lid is red granite, painted to match and cracked across — a hurried substitute.

pois.name: North wall
pois.blurb: Right: Ay, the next king, in a priest's leopard skin, opens the mouth of Tutankhamun's mummy. Centre: Nut greets the king. Left: the king and his ka are embraced by Osiris.

pois.name: West wall
pois.blurb: The first hour of the Amduat: twelve baboons, one for each hour of the night, below the sun-god as a scarab in his barque.

pois.name: East wall
pois.blurb: The funeral: twelve courtiers in white draw the sledge that carries the king's mummy under a canopy of garlands.

pois.name: South wall
pois.blurb: Hathor, mistress of the West, holds the sign of life to the king's nose; Anubis stands behind him. Only this western end survives — the rest was painted on the partition Carter took down. What you see here is a drawn reconstruction of the composition, not a photograph: no freely licensed photograph of this wall exists.

pois.name: Treasury
pois.blurb: The treasury, guarded by the Anubis shrine: it held the gilded canopic shrine, model boats and chests of jewellery.
